---
title: "Handson: equatorial ocean model"
---

We learn the basics of data assimilation (DA) using an equatorial ocean model [@Thacker-Long:1988].

## Governing equations

The domain is one-dimensional in the longitudinal direction ($x$) with a cyclic boundary condition.
The model consists of three linear waves.
Each wave propagates with a constant wave speed; the model is linear of form.

$$
\frac{\partial q_j}{\partial t} + c_j\frac{\partial q_j}{\partial x} + \sigma q_j = d_j f,\; j = 0,\,2,\,4
$$ {#eq-governing_equations}

The index $j = 0$  represents the Kelvin wave, which propagates eastward with the phase speed of $c_0 = 1$ and the sensitivity to forcing of $d_j = 1$.
The indices $j = 2, 4$ are the Rossby waves with $c_2 = - c_0/3,\,c_4 = -c_0/7$ and $d_2 = 1/2,\,d_4 = 1/8$, respectively.
The damping coefficient $\sigma$ is independent of the wave types.

The only observable is the sea-surface height.

$$
h = q_0 + q_2 - q_4
$$ {#eq-observation_operator}

## Discretization

The governing equations (@eq-governing_equations) is discretized with the Lax-Wendroff method [@Lax-Wendroff:1960].
This scheme is a single step and explicit method of $O(\tau^2)$, where $\tau$ is the time step.
The $O(\tau)$ error in time is elimiated in space.
Consider advection equation

$$
\frac{\partial q}{\partial t} + c\frac{\partial q}{\partial x} = 0,
$$ {#eq-advection}

which is discretized as

$$
\frac{q_j^{n+1} - q_j^n}{\tau} + c\frac{q_{j+1}^n - q_{j-1}^n}{2\Delta} =
\frac{c^2\tau}{2}\left(\frac{q_{j+1}^n - 2q_j^n + q_{j-1}^n}{\Delta^2}\right)
$$ {#eq-discretized_advection}

where $\Delta$ is the grid interval.

The right-hand side of (@eq-discretized_advection) is a discretized form of the trunction error

$$
\frac{\tau}{2}\frac{\partial^2 q}{\partial t^2} = \frac{\tau}{2}\frac{\partial}{\partial t}\left(-c\frac{\partial q}{\partial x}\right) = \frac{c^2\tau}{2}\frac{\partial^2 q}{\partial x^2}.
$$

Using the Lax-Wendroff method, (@eq-governing_equations) is discretized as

$$
q_{j, i}^n = \frac{1}{1 + \sigma \tau}\left\{
q_{j, i}^{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j(q_{j, i+1}^{n-1} - q_{j, i-1}^{n-1})
+ \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j^2(q_{j,i+1}^{n-1} - 2q_{j,i}^{n-1} + q_{j, i-1}^{n-1}) + \tau d_j f_i^n
\right\}
$$ {#eq-forward}
where $\gamma_j = c_j\tau/\Delta$.

## Lagrangian method

For simplicity, it is assumed that observations are available on the model grid and observations are uncorrelated one another.

The cost function can be defined as

$$
J = \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i = 0}^{I} \sum_{n = 0}^N [(\eta_i^n - h_i^n)^2 + (\phi_i^n - f_i^n)^2]
$$ {#eq-cost_function}

where $\eta_i^n, \phi_i^n$ are sea-surface height and wind stress observations and
$h_i^n = q_{0,i}^n + q_{2,i}^n - q_{4,i}^n, f_i^n$ are their model equivalents, respectively.

The Lagrangian function is defined as

$$
L = J + \sum_{j = 0}^{2, 4} \sum_{i = 0}^I \sum_{n=1}^N \lambda_{j, i}^n[
(1 + \sigma\tau)q_{j, i}^n - q_{j, i}^{n-1} + \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j(q_{j, i+1}^{n-1} - q_{j, i}^{n-1})
- \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j^2(q_{j,i+1}^{n-1} - 2q_{j, i}^{n-1} + q_{j, i-1}^{n-1}) - \tau d_j f_i^n]
$$ {#eq-lagrange_function}

Where $\lambda_{j,i}^n$ is the Lagrange multiplier (and adjoint variable) with the terminal and initial conditions

$$
\begin{aligned}
\lambda_{j,i}^{N+1} &= 0 \\
\lambda_{j,i}^0 &= 0. 
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-adjoint-bc}

The terminal condition indicates at the future step $n = N+1$, the adjoint is naught.
The initial condition is fulfilled at the minimizer; it is the negative gradient, used for optimization.

$\partial L/\partial \lambda_{j,i}^n$ recovers the forward model (@eq-forward).
$\partial L/\partial q_{j,i}^n$ leads to the adjoint equation

$$
\lambda_{j, i}^n = \frac{1}{1 + \sigma \tau}\left\{
\lambda_{j, i}^{n+1} - \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j(\lambda_{j, i-1}^{n+1} - \lambda_{j, i+1}^{n+1})
+ \frac{1}{2}\gamma_j^2(\lambda_{j,i-1}^{n+1} - 2\lambda_{j,i}^{n+1} + \lambda_{j, i+1}^{n+1})
+ \varepsilon_j(\eta_i^n - q_{0,i}^n - q_{2,i}^n + q_{4,i}^n)\right\}
$$ {#eq-adjoint}

where $\varepsilon_0 = \varepsilon_2 = 1, \varepsilon_4 = -1$.
The last term on the right-hand side exist at the step where the observations are available.
Finally, $\partial L/\partial f_i$ gives
$$
-\tau\sum_j d_j\lambda_{j,i}^n - (\phi_i^n - f_i^n) = 0
$$ {#eq-forcing_gradients}
at the minimizer.
The left-hand side of (@eq-forcing_gradients) represents the gradient with respect to forcing.

::: {.callout-note title = "Excercises for beginners"}
- Write the forward model and run the model with a prescribed two-cycle forcing migrating with $c_f = 0.5$.
- Derive the adjoint model and estimate the initial state with the observations at $n = 0. 16, 32$.
- Compare the gradient descent and conjugate gradient methods.
- Write an perturbed observation (PO) ensemble Kalman filter (EnKF) to assimilate observation sequentially.
- Add noise to the observations.
- Change the obsertion frequency and locations.
:::

::: {.callout-note title = "Excercises for intermediates"}
- Modify the variational method to estimate the forcing at all steps.
- Write (ensemble) Kalman smoother and compare with the variational method.
- Write a variational or ensemble data assimilation code for your favourite model, e.g. the Lorenz-96 model and its variants.
:::
